title: Rates, edges and settings
intro: The chapter above gave the counts. This level gives what a single swap trial actually is and what its failures contain, why the sparsity level has to be supplied by hand rather than derived, which of the band's two edges has support from outside the lens, and what the paper states it has not measured at all.

chapters.title: What one trial is
chapters.body:
A trial is one prompt, one edit, and one scored token.

The prompt applies a function to an argument: "the capital of France is", "most people in France speak", "France is on the continent of" ([[function-template-protocol]]). The edit is a [[lens-coordinate-swap]]. The activation's coordinates along the France vector and the China vector are read, exchanged, and written back, then held at that value at every token position across a band of middle layers ([[activation-clamping]]).

The edit is the same edit in every prompt. Nothing in it is tuned to the function it lands in. That identity is what makes the experiment a test of broadcast rather than sixteen separate steering results ([[prompt-independent-swap]], [[flexible-generalization]]).

Scoring is against the answer the prompt would have had if the swapped-in concept were the true one, not against the swapped-in concept itself ([[implied-counterfactual-answer]]). Under "the capital of ___ is", a trial with China swapped in counts as a success only when Beijing reaches top-1. The single worked case the paper prints is France to China across three functions at once ([[fig-18]]).

Each template's trials are laid out as a $4 \times 4$ grid, rows the argument written in the prompt and columns the argument swapped in ([[swap-grid-diagonal-baseline]]). The four diagonal cells exchange a vector for itself, so they are the unmodified run and are not counted. Twelve off-diagonal cells per template, four templates per category, gives 48 scored trials per category.

Country templates land on 42 of their 48 ([[fig-68]]). Number relations land on none of theirs. Months and animals divide the remaining 96 trials and succeed on 34 of them; the paper gives the ordering between those two categories rather than the two separate counts.

chapters.title: What a failed trial contains
chapters.body:
The 76 counts top-1 hits, and the cells it excludes are not empty.

In most failing cells the model's top-1 token is still the correct answer for the argument actually written in the prompt, while the target's answer sits somewhere below it; the grids print that position as a small grey rank ([[partial-swap-rank-evidence]]). Doubling the magnitude of the edit often brings it to the top ([[swap-strength-alpha]]).

The paper reads the rank and the recovery together as a swap that moved the activation the right way and not far enough.

That reading carries a cost. If the magnitude deciding the outcome is a free parameter of the intervention, a binary success rate at one setting of it is a fact about the intervention as much as about the model. Both settings are reported and neither is called the real one.

The right-hand panel of [[fig-19]] drops the binary. It plots, per trial, how far the swap shifted the output toward the target's answer ([[swap-effect-magnitude]]) against the source argument's [[workspace-loading]] — the [[cosine-similarity]] between the [[residual-stream]] and that concept's lens vector, averaged over the argument and readout positions of an unmodified pass. The relation there is continuous, and it runs in the same order as the categories.

One ambiguity is left standing. Elsewhere the paper reads a swap that changes nothing as evidence that the computation does not route through the workspace ([[null-swap-interpretation]]). Here the same null outcome is attributed instead to a concept that was barely in the workspace to begin with. Loading is what separates the two cases, and loading is measured with the same lens whose vectors the swap moves.

The second reading of the number-word result is not the multi-token problem ([[number-word-failure-interpretation]]). Number words are single tokens. What would be failing is the alignment between the model's working representation of a small integer and the lens vector for that integer's token ([[single-token-limitation]]).

chapters.title: The constant nobody derived
chapters.body:
The J-lens vectors do not fail to span the residual stream. At a given layer there is one per vocabulary entry, and the matrix formed by stacking them is full rank, so every activation is already some linear combination of them ([[j-space-formalization]]).

What makes the J-space a restriction is the sparsity level. Fix $k$, and the allowed points are the nonnegative combinations of any $k$ of the vectors: one polyhedral cone per choice of $k$ vectors, with the J-space their union ([[union-of-cones]]). The vectors coupled with that $k$ are what the paper names a [[sparse-subframe]].

Nothing in the construction supplies $k$. Until one is chosen there is no set for an activation to be inside or outside of. The paper states $k \approx 25$ as its usual value.

The measurement that agrees with it runs the other way round. [[sparse-decomposition]] fits an activation greedily with nonnegative combinations of lens vectors ([[gradient-pursuit]]), and the identical fit is run against a control set of random directions of the same size. [[j-space-occupancy]] is the count at which one more lens vector stops beating one more random direction. It is near zero through the early layers and plateaus near 25 across the band in the median case, with a wide percentile spread over positions ([[fig-30]]).

Two things keep the agreement looser than it looks. Occupancy counts active vectors rather than ideas, and several vectors can jointly stand for one broader category ([[vectors-versus-concepts]]). And $k$ is not a single number across the paper: ablation projects out the top ten directions, while the word-list experiment counts a word present if it reaches the top 25 ([[sparsity-level-k]]).

The formalization was not written to fix $k$. It was written so that two candidate workspaces, built by different methods or over different vocabularies, can be compared by the reconstruction error they assign to the same activations ([[workspace-candidate]]).

chapters.title: Both edges, and what fixed them
chapters.childScope: Take the band's evidence apart one piece at a time: the four lens-derived boundary statistics and what each would look like if the band were not there ([[workspace-boundary-metrics]], [[fig-28]]); the CKA layer-similarity matrix and the subsampling that sharpens its blocks ([[cka]], [[layer-subsampling]]); the two competing accounts of the empty early band ([[sensory-layers]], [[early-layer-lens-degeneracy]]); and the lens-free ambiguity sweep that gives the onset independent support ([[fig-29]], [[ignition]], [[transition-width]]).
chapters.body:
Four statistics fix the band, and all four change at the same two depths ([[workspace-boundary-metrics]]): how often a top-$k$ lens token matches the model's own next-token prediction ([[lens-next-token-accuracy]]), how sharply peaked a readout is on a few tokens ([[readout-excess-kurtosis]]), how often the same token stays on top from one position to the next ([[top1-autocorrelation]]), and how many residual-stream dimensions the lens vectors need between them ([[j-space-effective-dimensionality]]).

Their agreement is weaker evidence than four independent agreements would be. All four are computed from the lens. Content the lens cannot resolve at a given depth goes missing from every one of them at once.

[[cka]] compares two layers by their matrices of pairwise similarities among lens vectors, and it separates an early block from a long middle one. That establishes the early layers as a coherent regime of their own. It does not say which account of them is right. The apparent sharpness of the block edges is also inflated by running the analysis on subsampled layers ([[layer-subsampling]]).

One measurement at the onset does not come from the lens. A concept token's input embedding is replaced by a weighted mixture of two countries' embeddings ([[embedding-mixture-experiment]]), and the resulting activation is scored by where it sits on the line joining that same trial's two pure endpoints ([[projection-share]]). Early layers track the mixture smoothly. From about the onset layer the share sits at one endpoint or the other, switching at a threshold ([[fig-29]]).

The onset is therefore visible to something other than the lens.

The late edge has no equivalent check. There the averaged Jacobian approaches the identity and the readout collapses toward the plain unembedding projection ([[jacobian-approaches-identity]]). Calling those layers [[motor-layers]] is in part a statement about what the instrument can still distinguish.

chapters.title: The questions left standing
chapters.body:
The [[open-questions]] section separates what was tested from what was not.

One cause is ruled out. The workspace is present and load-bearing in the [[base-model]], before any reinforcement learning from human feedback ([[post-training]]), so it is not something Assistant training installs.

What would replace that hypothesis is not measured. The models studied are large production models at the end of training. Whether the workspace forms early or late in pretraining, whether it arrives gradually or abruptly, and whether a small model has an equally rich workspace, a proportionally smaller one, a less reliable one, or none, are all untested.

No mechanism is given for what puts a representation in. The same information sits in the workspace or outside it depending on what the model is asked to do with it, which the paper reads as some analog of attentional selection without identifying what performs the selection ([[attentional-selection-analog]]).

Nor is there a criterion that predicts engagement in advance. The [[flexible-vs-automatic-dissociation]] holds that the workspace is engaged when an intermediate must be handed to an arbitrary, context-specified consumer, and bypassed when the computation is automatic. The tasks it was tested on were chosen because that distinction is clear for them. For an arbitrary computation the paper states it cannot predict which side the computation falls on ([[automaticity-criterion-limits]]).

That gap bears directly on the safety use of the lens. A misaligned behavior practiced into a fixed circuit would run without surfacing in a readout at all, which is the limit on reading a model's intentions this way ([[automatic-misalignment-blind-spot]], [[alignment-auditing]]).
